title: Latitude Degree Distance Calculator
description: Convert a latitude difference to approximate north-south distance using 111.195 km per degree. Worked examples, units and limitations explained.
summary_sentence: A difference of 0.9° gives 100.0755 km before rounding, using the calculator’s constant 111.195 km-per-degree scale.
quick_answer: This calculator multiplies the absolute latitude difference by 111.195 to estimate kilometres, and by 69.093 to estimate miles. It uses a constant mean-Earth scale, not a latitude-dependent ellipsoidal calculation. The reference field does not change this conversion. Use it for quick north-south scale estimates rather than legal measurements.
steps_intro: Subtract the two latitude values, preserving their signs when calculating the difference. Enter that angular difference, then read the distance. The tool uses the absolute size of the difference; it does not report northbound or southbound travel.

use_cases.title: Estimate the height of a study area

body.t: A dataset bounded by 40.0°N and 40.9°N spans 0.9 degrees of latitude. Converting that span to approximately 100.076 km gives a useful sense of its north-south size before opening a GIS project. This is the height implied by the bounding latitudes, not the length of an irregular boundary or the distance along a road. Keep the original coordinates with the reported estimate so another reader can check the input.

use_cases.title: Check coordinate units before an import

body.t: A coordinate column containing 0.01-degree steps is not describing points ten metres apart. Under this model, 0.01 degrees of latitude is about 1.112 km. This simple check can catch a unit assumption before a dataset is imported into a mapping application. It does not tell you whether the source coordinates are accurate, whether they use the expected datum, or whether a missing minus sign has placed them in the wrong hemisphere.

use_cases.title: Describe the scale of a gridded dataset

body.t: Latitude bands provide one dimension of an angular grid. Converting the band height helps explain a climate or terrain raster in familiar units, but it does not establish the area of a cell. The east-west width also depends on latitude. Pair this calculation with a longitude conversion rather than assuming that a cell measuring one degree by one degree is a square on the ground. For area statistics, use the dataset’s documented area method.

use_cases.title: Separate north-south change from total separation

body.t: Two locations can have nearly identical latitudes while still being thousands of kilometres apart east to west. This calculator measures only the latitude component, so a small result does not mean the locations are close. Use it to describe north-south extent, then use a two-point distance calculator when the question is actual surface separation. A driving route introduces another distinction because roads do not follow the geometric shortest path.

From −0.2° to +0.3°, the latitude difference is 0.5°, not 0.1°. The estimate is 0.5 × 111.195 = 55.5975 km, displayed as about 55.598 km. Compute the signed subtraction first, then take its magnitude. Adding the absolute coordinates happens to work for opposite hemispheres but would be incorrect for two points in the same hemisphere.

A latitude step of 0.00001° corresponds to 0.00111195 km, or approximately 1.112 metres under the model. That describes the spacing between coordinate values, not GPS accuracy. A device reading can show five decimals while the physical location is uncertain by several metres. Do not use the number of displayed decimals as a substitute for a measurement accuracy specification.

popular_table.title: Latitude differences using this calculator’s scale
popular_table.intro: Calculated as absolute degrees × 111.195 km. These are mean-scale estimates, not ellipsoidal degree lengths at different latitudes.
popular_table.note: The implementation also uses 69.093 miles per degree. Small differences can occur if a rounded kilometre output is converted separately to miles.

faq: Does the reference field change the answer?

No. The current latitude-span implementation uses a fixed distance per degree and does not use the reference value in its calculation. It should not be described as a latitude-aware ellipsoidal solver.
Is one degree of latitude exactly 111.195 km?

Not on the real ellipsoidal Earth. The calculator uses a convenient mean scale. Actual meridional degree length varies with latitude, so surveying and precise geographic analysis need a suitable geodesic method.
Can I use negative latitude differences?

The output uses the absolute magnitude. A negative difference therefore produces the same estimated distance as the equivalent positive difference. Keep direction separately if your workflow needs it.
Can I estimate a whole meridian with this tool?

The arithmetic will scale a large angular span, but it remains the same constant-scale approximation. It does not integrate the varying degree length along an ellipsoid. Do not quote that result as an exact pole-to-pole measurement.
What if both coordinates are south of the equator?
Use signed decimal coordinates when subtracting. For −35° and −34.5°, the difference is 0.5°. The fact that both points are south does not change the magnitude of the span.
Which tool should I use for full point-to-point distance?

Use Distance Between Two Places when both latitude and longitude change. This calculator deliberately isolates one coordinate dimension; it cannot determine a complete journey from a latitude difference alone.
